newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Waigel sticks to strict line on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Waigel sticks to strict line on EMU.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Saturday renewed a tough commitment to a strict interpretation of entry criteria for European monetary union (EMU), dispelling talk that he had relaxed his position.

At a conference of his Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats which ended on Saturday, Waigel said Maastricht Treaty limits meant European Union nations must have a budget deficit below 3.0 percent of gross domestic product to qualify for EMU.
"I have said the goal is to be three and not three plus x," Waigel told reporters, continuing tough rhetoric which had not been heard in months until the CSU conference.
CSU delegates late on Friday approved a motion amending their party policy to call for a budget limit of "3.0 percent" of GDP rather than the less exact "three percent".

Recently Waigel had stopped calling for a precise three percent, preferring to speak only of "three percent", which some independent economists had interpreted as meaning Germany could live with a few points behind the decimal point.

The quibbling over exactly what "three" means has become a central point of political debate about EMU in Germany as high unemployment and fragile growth place a question mark over Bonn's ability to meet its 2.9 percent deficit target this year.
Waigel insisted in his speech to the conference: "Germany will fulfil the criteria, contrary to any doubt by some."

European government leaders will determine which nations meet the deficit, debt, and other entry criteria to join EMU after evaluating 1997 economic data early next year. EMU is scheduled to begin in 1999.
Independent economists have said Germany could still hit the three percent budget deficit target on the nose, as long as growth picks up during the rest of the year.
To accelerate growth, and tackle Germany's most pressing problem, an 11.7 percent jobless rate, Waigel said Bonn's ambitious tax reform package must be pushed through soon.
"Anyone who blocks the tax reform is partly to blame if no new jobs are created," Waigel said, adding: "We need the tax reform now as a positive signal for investment."
Waigel also urged employers to create new jobs now.

Three days before the ruling coalition resumes talks on the tax reform package with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), Waigel accused SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine of souring the public mood with obstructionist policies and suggestions.
"I have the impression that Lafontaine is only interested in creating a mood and not really interested in Germany's welfare," he said.
